name: LMR33630ADDAR
title: 3.8 V to 36 V, 3 A synchronous step-down converter
summary: The LMR33630 is a synchronous buck converter with both power MOSFETs on chip, running from 3.8 V to 36 V and delivering up to 3 A at an adjustable 1 V to 24 V output. It uses peak-current-mode control with internal compensation and comes in fixed 400 kHz, 1.4 MHz and 2.1 MHz versions. At light load it moves to PFM and draws about 25 µA in regulation. It has a precision enable, a power-good flag, soft start, cycle-by-cycle and hiccup current limiting, UVLO and thermal shutdown, in an 8-pin HSOIC with thermal pad or a 12-pin 3 × 2 mm VQFN-HR.

pins.name: PGND
pins.function: Power ground, the return of the low-side switch. Join it to system ground and AGND; the input bypass capacitor connects to it with short, wide copper.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input of the converter. The input bypass capacitors go straight across this pin and PGND.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable: high runs the converter, low turns it off. Its precise threshold allows a resistor divider from VIN to set a higher turn-on voltage. It may be tied to VIN, and must never be left floating.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power-good flag. High when the output is within its window, low on a fault and whenever EN is low. Pull it up to a suitable supply through a current-limiting resistor; may be left unconnected when unused.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input, taken from the tap of the output voltage divider. Must be neither left floating nor grounded.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: Output of the internal 5 V regulator that runs the control circuits. Takes a 1 µF ceramic capacitor to ground. Not for outside loads, except that it may supply the power-good pull-up.

pins.name: BOOT
pins.function: Supply of the high-side gate driver. A 100 nF ceramic capacitor connects from this pin to SW.

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node, the connection to the power inductor.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Exposed thermal pad, which is also the analog ground: the reference for the internal references and logic, against which every electrical figure is measured. Solder it to a ground plane for both electrical and thermal performance.

pins.name: PGND
pins.function: Power ground, one pin on each side of the package. Join to system ground and AGND; each input bypass capacitor connects to its PGND pin with short, wide copper.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input, one pin on each side, each paired with a PGND pin so the input capacitors can be split across both sides. Join both on the board.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable: high runs the converter, low turns it off. May be tied to VIN; must never float.

pins.name: PG
pins.function: Power-good flag, high when the output is in regulation and low on a fault or when EN is low. Pull up through a current-limiting resistor; may be left open when unused.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input from the output divider tap. Must be neither floating nor grounded.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: Internal 5 V regulator output for the control circuits; 1 µF ceramic capacitor to ground. Not for outside loads apart from the power-good pull-up.

pins.name: AGND
pins.function: Analog ground and reference for all electrical figures; connect to system ground on the board.

pins.name: BOOT
pins.function: High-side gate-driver supply; 100 nF ceramic capacitor from this pin to SW. Routing SW to the neighbouring NC pin on the board brings the switch node next to BOOT for this capacitor.

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node, to the power inductor. Connect it to NC (pin 3) on the board.

pins.name: NC
pins.function: No internal connection. Joined to SW on the board so that the boot capacitor can reach the switch node beside BOOT.

circuits.title: Example application, 5 V 3 A at 400 kHz
circuits.description: A 400 kHz step-down converter taking 6 V to 36 V down to 5 V at up to 3 A. EN is tied to VIN so the part runs whenever the input is present. R1 and R2 divide the output onto FB (1 V reference), C3 feeds the high-side driver from SW, C4 holds the internal 5 V rail, and R3 pulls the power-good flag up to that rail. C1 carries the input ripple current while C2 sits right at the pins for high-frequency bypass. The inductor is sized for about 30 % ripple, and the output bank for a 250 mV deviation on a 2 A load step.

operation.text: Synchronous buck converter with both power switches inside, peak-current-mode control and internal loop compensation. It can turn 20 V into 3.3 V at 2.1 MHz, and hold a 3.3 V output from as little as 3.8 V in. The VQFN package places VIN and PGND pins symmetrically on two sides, so the input current loops on the two sides partly cancel their magnetic fields, lowering EMI; its small parasitic inductance also limits switch-node ringing.

One silicon in three fixed switching frequencies (A 400 kHz, B 1.4 MHz, C 2.1 MHz) and two packages (8-pin HSOIC with thermal pad, 12-pin VQFN-HR with wettable flanks). All are rated 3 A with an adjustable output. A separate AEC-Q100 automotive version is the LMR33630-Q1. The part is functional-safety capable.

PG is an open-drain NMOS that pulls low when the output leaves the window set by the VPG thresholds, on faults such as current limit and thermal shutdown, and during start-up. Excursions shorter than the glitch filter time tPG are ignored. At first power-up the flag rises about 4 ms (typ) after EN is asserted; this delay appears only at start-up. Pull it up to a logic supply, or to VCC or VOUT through 100 kΩ; leave the pin unconnected if unused. Driving EN low forces PG low, and with EN low the flag stays valid while VIN is at least about 2 V. Keep the DC current into PG below 5 mA. Its current is limited inside to roughly 35 mA when enabled and 65 mA when disabled, which protects it while discharging a filter capacitor on the pin.

EN has two levels. Above VEN-VCC-H the internal VCC regulator starts but the output stays off (standby). At VEN-H the converter starts with soft start. Falling VEN-HYS below VEN-H returns it to standby, and below VEN-VCC-L it shuts down completely. The precise VEN-H threshold lets a divider from VIN set a custom input undervoltage lockout. EN may be tied straight to VIN but must not float.
Start-up follows an internal reference ramp, which avoids output overshoot and large inrush current. The output rises in about 4 ms (tSS).

Both the peak and the valley of the inductor current are limited. When an overload keeps the valley current above ILIMIT at the next clock edge, that cycle is skipped, so the frequency drops and the ripple grows. When the peak then reaches ISC, the duty cycle is cut and the output falls out of regulation; this sets the maximum output current. A zero-current detector on the low-side switch (threshold IZC) provides diode emulation at light load.

If FB falls below about 0.4 V while the part is in current limit, switching stops for tHC (about 94 ms), then the part restarts with soft start. If the short is still there it runs in current limit for about 20 ms and stops again, repeating while the fault lasts. This keeps the part cooler and greatly reduces output current during a hard short; once the short is removed the output comes back normally after the hiccup delay. The 0.4 V detection is not active in dropout.

Lockout watches VCC, the internal regulator output. The part is ready to start at about 3.7 V on VCC and shuts down below about 3 V whatever EN says. Because the regulator is in dropout at these points, the same figures roughly apply to the input voltage.
The part stops at a junction temperature of about 165 °C and restarts when it has cooled to about 148 °C.

The converter changes mode with load. At heavy load it runs PWM at constant frequency, with good line and load regulation and low ripple. At light load it runs PFM: the high-side switch fires in bursts of one or more pulses, each lasting until the inductor current reaches IPEAK-MIN, and the bursts are spaced to regulate, with diode emulation. PFM keeps efficiency high at light load but gives more ripple, a load-dependent frequency and a slight rise in output voltage. The load at the changeover depends on input voltage, inductance and nominal frequency, and is higher at higher frequency; the mode-change curves are for the RNX parts list at 400 kHz. Where the frequency must be known, test the transition before finalising the design.

As VIN approaches VOUT, the off-time nears its minimum. The part then lowers its frequency to extend the duty cycle and stay in regulation. Dropout voltage is taken as VIN - VOUT when the output has sagged 1 % below nominal; at that point the frequency has reached its floor of about 140 kHz. Dropout is set by the switch on-resistances, the inductor DC resistance and the maximum duty cycle.

At high input and low output voltage the on-time reaches its minimum; the part then keeps the on-time fixed and reduces the frequency, so the lowest output voltage can still be regulated from the highest input voltage.
A lower frequency gives lower switching loss and usually higher efficiency; a higher one allows a smaller inductor and output capacitors. The example uses 400 kHz.

The output is set by RFBT and RFBB on FB, regulated to the 1 V reference. Low resistor values resist noise pickup but cost light-load efficiency. RFBT is best 100 kΩ and at most 1 MΩ; at 1 MΩ a feedforward capacitor across RFBT is needed for phase margin. The 5 V example uses 100 kΩ and 24.9 kΩ.

Choose ripple of 20 % to 40 % of the maximum output current, 30 % being best; when the load is far below what the part can supply, still use the part's maximum current. The saturation current should ideally reach the high-side limit ISC so the inductor does not saturate in a short circuit, and must never be below the low-side limit ILIMIT; a saturating inductor lets current rise very fast and can cause damage. Ferrite cores saturate hard but have lower core loss; powdered-iron cores saturate softly but lose more above about 1 MHz. The inductance is capped by the need for ripple of at least about 10 % of rated current.

Capacitance values mean effective capacitance under DC bias and temperature. Use low-ESR ceramics of X5R or better. High-value ceramics lose much of their capacitance under bias; larger cases and higher voltage ratings lose less, and parallel parts help reach the minimum and share RMS current.

Size the bank for the load transient first, then check ripple. The 5 V example needs 52 µF and 0.11 Ω; allowing 20 % tolerance and 10 % bias derating gives 72 µF, met by four 22 µF 16 V ceramics in 1210. An aluminium electrolytic may be added in parallel. Rate capacitors at 10 V or more for outputs of 3.3 V or less, and 16 V or more for 5 V and above. Small ceramics of 1 nF to 100 nF on the output cut voltage spikes from inductor and board parasitics. Total output capacitance should be held to about 10× the design value, or to 1000 µF if that is less, since more can upset start-up and loop stability. Confirm the design with load-transient tests and Bode plots before production.

At least 10 µF of ceramic capacitance is required at the input, rated for at least the highest input voltage and preferably twice it. A small-case 220 nF ceramic must also sit as close to the part as possible to bypass its internal control circuits; in the example it is 50 V X7R, beside a 4.7 µF 50 V X7R. On the VQFN, the two VIN/PGND pairs on opposite sides let the input capacitors be split; the example puts one 4.7 µF and two 100 nF at each pair. An electrolytic in parallel damps ringing from long supply leads and supports the input during dips from a high-impedance source.
A 100 nF ceramic rated 10 V or more between BOOT and SW powers the gate drivers.
VCC needs a 1 µF 16 V ceramic to ground. It is nominally 5 V. Avoid loading it, except that it may supply the power-good pull-up (100 kΩ suits); never short it to ground or another voltage.
A capacitor across RFBT can improve load-transient response or phase margin, mainly when RFBT exceeds 100 kΩ, where the large resistor and the FB pin capacitance form a pole that disturbs stability.

The die must stay at or below 125 °C, which limits the dissipation and so the load current. The effective RθJA depends on dissipation, air flow, board area, copper area, thermal vias and nearby parts. The HSOIC's thermal pad must be soldered to heatsinking copper; the VQFN has no die-attach pad and so a higher RθJA. The RθJA-against-copper-area curves give the area of each layer of a board with 2 oz outer and 1 oz inner copper; the output current curves were taken at the stated RθJA.

The source must deliver the input current of the loaded converter. Long leads add inductance that can ring with the ceramic input capacitors and overshoot, and resistance that can dip the input on a load step, possibly resetting the part near minimum input. Shorter leads or an aluminium or tantalum capacitor of 20 µF to 100 µF in parallel with the ceramics damp this. An input filter can cause instability unless designed with care. A snap-back (thyristor-type) TVS on the input is not recommended: if it clamps below the output voltage, the output capacitors discharge back through the part. The input must not fall below the output; otherwise the output capacitors discharge through the body diode between VIN and SW, uncontrolled. Where that can happen, a Schottky diode from the output back to the input supply is called for.

Do not exceed the absolute maximum, ESD or recommended operating ratings; never let EN float; never let the output rise above the input or fall below ground; do not design with the RθJA of the thermal table.

The input capacitor to VIN and PGND loop carries the fast current edges: keep it as small as possible with short, wide copper. Place the input capacitors right at VIN and GND; on the VQFN use both VIN/PGND pairs and join them with a wide VIN plane on a lower layer. Put the VCC capacitor close to VCC and GND with short, wide traces. Keep CBOOT close with short, wide traces to BOOT and SW; on the VQFN run SW under the part to the NC pin and connect CBOOT through that path. Place RFBT, RFBB and any CFF close to FB with short connections to FB and ground; the line to VOUT may be longer but must stay away from SW and other noise sources. Use at least one inner ground plane as shield and heat path. Solder the HSOIC thermal pad to the ground plane with an array of thermal vias to the bottom layer and inner planes. Make VIN, VOUT and GND paths wide and direct. Give enough copper area for heatsinking; outer layers 2 oz, and no less than 1 oz. Keep the SW copper short, wide and small in area to limit radiated EMI.

Connect AGND and PGND to the ground planes with vias beside the bypass capacitors. PGND ties directly to the low-side switch source and the input and output capacitor grounds, and carries switching noise. Keep PGND, VIN and SW routing on one side of the ground plane and sensitive routing on the other, quieter side. Under the thermal pad use at least a 4 × 3 array of evenly spread 10-mil vias to the ground plane. A four-layer board with 2 oz / 1 oz / 1 oz / 2 oz copper is recommended.
